This game has its strengths and weaknesses, and actually, one weakness is so bad that it’s good.

To be honest, this VR title feels more like a tech demo than a full-fledged game. It’s a mix of different modes that feel like the developer wanted to say: "Hey, look what kind of games you can make in VR!"

The primary mode is a tower defense game with multiple levels. It’s okay overall; some maps are well-designed and require a tactical approach, while others are quite boring. The extra modes are fine too.

But on my playthrough, I found out the hard way why this game could have it's title "Out of Ammo". It’s not just a title; it’s a promise caused by a bug. For some reason, you occasionally can't grab specific objects, which makes situations, like reloading, luck based. While this is a terrible control issue, it made the game significantly harder, especially in the final extra mission. I’d be lying if I said that this ironic "feature" didn't feel like a cool, unintended challenge.

If you can laugh it off like I did, you can actually have fun with this experimental title. But don't be frustrated if you have difficulties trying to grab and put a new magazine, while you are literally out of ammo. XD

Out of Ammo, developed and published by RocketWerkz, is a distinctive virtual reality title that merges real-time strategy with first-person shooter mechanics, delivering a hybrid gameplay experience that feels both dynamic and immersive. Set in a voxel-style battlefield, players are tasked with defending their base against waves of increasingly challenging enemies. The game’s appeal lies in its ability to seamlessly combine strategic planning with direct, hands-on combat, creating a layered experience that requires both tactical thinking and quick reflexes.

The gameplay in Out of Ammo revolves around a dual approach. In the strategic mode, players act as a commander, placing defensive structures such as bunkers, turrets, and sniper towers while managing resources and positioning troops. This layer of planning requires foresight and adaptability, as players must anticipate enemy paths and balance limited supplies to fortify their defenses effectively. Once the battlefield is prepared, players can jump into first-person mode, taking control of individual soldiers to actively engage enemies, shoot from cover, and physically interact with the environment. This combination of macro-level strategy and micro-level action ensures that no two encounters feel the same, keeping the gameplay fresh and engaging.

One of the game’s most compelling features is its full exploitation of VR capabilities. The room-scale design allows players to physically move around their play area, crouch behind cover, and manipulate objects directly with motion controllers. Building fortifications, aiming weapons, and issuing commands all benefit from the tactile, immersive interaction that VR provides, making the player feel truly present on the battlefield. This level of immersion elevates the gameplay, turning traditional RTS and FPS elements into a physically engaging and satisfying experience.

Visually, the game adopts a voxel-based art style that is both functional and charming. While it lacks photorealism, the colorful, blocky design provides clarity during fast-paced combat, allowing players to quickly identify enemies, structures, and environmental hazards. The environments are varied, featuring different terrains and layouts that add tactical depth and encourage creative use of defensive structures. Complementing the visuals, the audio design enhances immersion with realistic weapon sounds, environmental effects, and subtle cues that alert players to incoming threats, reinforcing the sense of being in an active combat zone.

Content-wise, Out of Ammo offers multiple layers of engagement. The campaign mode presents progressively difficult missions that challenge both strategic thinking and combat proficiency. A freeplay mode allows players to experiment with custom scenarios, testing new strategies or simply enjoying chaotic battles. Cooperative multiplayer adds further depth, enabling friends to team up and coordinate tactics, which not only increases replayability but also introduces a social, collaborative element to the experience.

Despite its many strengths, the game does have some limitations. Some players may find the pacing uneven, as the transition between strategic planning and active combat can occasionally feel abrupt. Additionally, the AI can sometimes behave unpredictably, with enemies failing to act in expected ways, which can disrupt carefully laid plans. While these issues do not fundamentally undermine the game, they can occasionally hinder the otherwise fluid experience.

Overall, Out of Ammo stands out as an innovative VR title that successfully bridges the gap between strategy and action. Its combination of immersive room-scale interaction, tactical planning, and direct combat creates a compelling experience that is both challenging and rewarding. Though not without minor flaws, the game’s unique approach, replayable content, and engaging mechanics make it a noteworthy entry in the VR landscape, appealing to fans of strategy, shooters, and immersive virtual experiences alike.

[h1]“Out of Ammo? More Like Out of Control – And I Loved It”[/h1]

I went in expecting a chill VR strategy game. You know—place a few soldiers, defend a base, sip some coffee. [Strike]Ten minutes later[/Strike] I’m screaming orders, flailing grenades, crawling on my floor trying to reload while my virtual medic gets sniped in the kidneys. This game is like babysitting a bunch of armed toddlers in a sandbox full of explosives—and somehow, it’s beautiful.

[hr][/hr]
[h3]Strategy Meets Chaos (And Then They Both Explode)[/h3]
You’re not just the commander here—you’re also the sniper, the builder, the guy frantically shoving magazines into empty rifles while enemies rush the gate. It’s tower defense, yes, but also full-body VR absurdity. One moment you’re placing sandbags like Bob the Builder with PTSD, the next you’re manually headshotting cardboard-faced soldiers with your shaky VR aim and a dream.

[hr][/hr]
[h3]Possession Is 9/10ths of the Battlefield[/h3]
One of the wildest parts? You can possess your units. Wanna be the sniper? Boom, you're the sniper. Wanna man the MG nest? Now you're the MG nest. It’s like playing chess, then standing up, kicking the bishop off the board, and becoming the knight yourself. You are the knight now. Deal with it.

[hr][/hr]
[h3]Low-Poly War Crimes (Aesthetic Edition)[/h3]
Visually? It looks like Minecraft and Medal of Honor had an awkward baby—and then forgot to give it a texture budget. But honestly? That low-poly charm grows on you. Watching blocky enemies ragdoll into the dirt after a perfectly timed artillery strike is… art. Cubic, pixelated, slightly cursed art.

[hr][/hr]
[h3]The Gameplay Loop of “Just One More Wave”[/h3]
The missions are short, but intense. You place units, reinforce the base, then desperately try to survive waves of attackers that get smarter, meaner, and more likely to drop you mid-respawn. It’s addictive in that “laughing while crying” kind of way. One minute you're a strategic genius, the next your entire frontline is on fire and you're hiding in a trench wondering if you left the oven on.

[hr][/hr]
[h3]What I Loved[/h3]
– The absurd joy of switching from commander to soldier mid-fight
– Manually reloading in VR while under fire = peak chaos fun
– Grenade tossing is an art. A very imprecise, hilarious art.
– Watching my squad actually hold the line... before all dying simultaneously

[hr][/hr]
[h3]What Could Be Better[/h3]
– It’s janky. Like, “Is that guy floating or just having a moment?” janky
– Content’s a bit light—after a few maps and modes, you’ve seen it all
– Controls can go from “immersive” to “WHAT IS HAPPENING” real quick
– AI is about as sharp as a soup spoon with a helmet

[hr][/hr]
[b]Final Thoughts:[/b]
Out of Ammo is the kind of game that feels like a fever dream cooked up by a sleep-deprived general and a VR dev with a caffeine problem. It’s buggy. It’s limited. It’s occasionally unfair. And yet, it’s a hilarious blast of pure VR adrenaline. Like tower defense met improv comedy—and both brought grenades.

[b]Final Score: 7.2/10[/b]

From the promo videos I really didn't think this game was going to be all that special, but at $12 CDN?  I decided to go ahead and give it a whirl anyway.  Boy, was I surprised.

The interactivity of the "menu" is pretty awesome.  It's basically an HQ tent on a firing range with everything you need to manipulate your game.  It's got a PC for checking multiplayer, a scoreboard on an overhead projector, mission map and... like I said, a firing range.  After you pass the tutorial mission all of these things become active and you can play around in this "main menu" area for hours just fooling about.

The game itself is played in two forms.  Your first form is basically a "god" where you tell your units where to build and where to stand.  You can call out orders for artillery strikes, helicopter strafing runs, and even sniper shots while having a birds-eye view of the battlefield.  The second stage is "possession" mode, where your god form basically possesses one of the ground units and you get into the battle first-hand.  You can't really move around, you're fairly stationary, but you have full control of shooting, reloading, and taking out the waves of attackers.  When you run out of ammo, you lose possession of your unit and go back to "god" mode.

There are quite a few levels in this game, and I feel more will be added as time goes on.  In addition once you beat a level it becomes available to you on "endless" mode, where you basically just see how many waves you can take on before you're wiped out.  While the maps all had the same theme, defend your HQ, they were all very different and the defence you used on the last map wouldn't work on the next one.  Each map required you to think out of the box as to how you wanted to defend your HQ... and your units.

Multiplayer is kind of a mixed bag.  I'd like to see players capable of joining you in the actual HQ "menu" tent, using it like a lobby, instead of them having to wait till you're already playing the mission (and your first wave of enemies is on the way).  Other than that I really like multiplayer in this game.  I found it worked best if one person played "god" and called out enemy approaches, while setting up defences, and the other players took over units on the field.  Of course, having more than one "god" at times also works, but you can quickly find yourselves stepping on each other's toes when assigning units and putting up defences.  Best to assign someone as the proverbial squad leader, and have everyone else focus on shooting the enemy waves.

One slight issue I noticed with this game is eye strain.  I don't know if it's the refresh rate or something else, but after about an hour of playing I found my eyes starting to get sore.  I don't have this problem in other games like Beat Sabre so I assume it's something with this specific game, although I can't confirm that as of yet.  I use an Oculus Quest 2, which works beautifully for most rift games, so I doubt that's the cause either.

All in all, yes I recommend this game.  At $12 CDN it's a bargain for what it offers, considering other games in it's class cost more than twice that.
